tagline: Oak-lined roads connect river settlements, a surviving church and a railroad town.
intro: The Historic Effingham-Ebenezer Scenic Byway covers 60 miles of state and local roads through oak-lined streets, grasslands and river country. Near Clyo, fields of corn, soybeans, peanuts and cotton interrupt the forest; farther south, oaks arch over Honey Ridge Road. Georgia DOT presents this state scenic byway as a journey through Effingham County’s history, including Ebenezer’s settlement by German Lutherans seeking religious freedom.

A local scenic-byway committee developed the corridor management plan, with Linda McDaniel of the Effingham County Chamber of Commerce leading the planning effort. In May 2007, four public meetings brought the proposal to Guyton, Springfield, Rincon and Meldrim. More than 2,000 letters notified property owners along the route. The committee’s stated aim was to preserve and share the county’s cultural, natural and historic resources. The route avoids industrial and commercial areas where possible.

Begin on Fourth Street in Rincon, head north, then take Highway 275 east to Ebenezer. Return west to Long Bridge Road for Ebenezer Creek, then continue through Clyo to the Savannah River ferry sites. The route doubles back toward Springfield and Guyton, reaches the Ogeechee River, then returns to Honey Ridge Road. Highway 17 and US 80 lead onward to Meldrim Road and the finish on Bay Street.
notice: Honey Ridge Road passes beneath a canopy of overhanging oaks.

moments.title: Jerusalem Lutheran Church
moments.text: Jerusalem Lutheran Church survived the decline of the town that built it. Completed in 1769, it is one of the few surviving buildings in Ebenezer. Salzburger Protestant refugees established Ebenezer in 1734 after expulsion from their homeland. With James Oglethorpe’s consent, the settlement moved closer to the Savannah River in 1736. The British invasion of 1778 severely damaged the town. County business later shifted to Springfield, and Ebenezer was abandoned by 1855. The church and townsite entered the National Register together in 1974. The Georgia Salzburger Society maintains its headquarters in historic Ebenezer and operates a research library and museum.

moments.title: Ebenezer Creek
moments.text: Long Bridge Road crosses a landscape of black water and cypress swamp at Ebenezer Creek. On December 9, 1864, Union troops under Brigadier General Jefferson C. Davis crossed the creek on a pontoon bridge. Davis had forbidden more than 600 people escaping slavery from crossing with them. After the soldiers crossed, his engineers cut the bridge loose. Many of those left behind drowned trying to reach the other bank. In 2010, the Georgia Historical Society erected a marker near the site to recognize the tragedy. Some Union soldiers tried to help from the eastern bank, while refugees built a raft to carry others across.

moments.title: Guyton
moments.text: Guyton’s lots and streets follow a survey made after the county took over Zachariah White’s land for unpaid taxes. White had granted a railroad right-of-way before his death in 1838. The county auctioned the property, and affluent Savannah residents bought many lots for summer homes during a yellow-fever epidemic. The railroad called the community Station Number 30. Residents wanted a name that would allow them to request a post office; because Georgia already had a Whitesville, railroad president W. W. Gordon chose Guyton, honoring local resident Archibald Guyton. A post office opened on December 31, 1851.
